title: What should the national Democratic education plan really look like?
author: Josh Cowen
source: The Forum with Josh Cowen (joshcowen.substack.com), September 25, 2026
summary: Josh Cowen, a voucher critic who has testified in 25 mostly red and purple states, argues that progressive Democratic candidates are missing a serious education agenda even as the issue dominates Republican politics. Warning that deficits may squeeze federal education spending, he calls for a strategic plan built on five themes. Democrats should defend public education by improving it, including restructuring the new federal scholarship tax credit and restoring civil rights enforcement. They should rebuild federal capacity to measure learning through NAEP, state assessments, and research, while abandoning the progressive temptation to treat measurement as suspect. He also urges a relentless focus on reading, math, attendance, and a real plan for AI, and argues Democrats should embrace choice within the public sector by building public schools good enough that families want to choose them. His bottom line is that excellence is one of the ways to achieve equity.
points: Cowen proposes that private schools funded by the federal scholarship credit follow the same testing and accountability rules as public schools.
He calls for restoring the gutted Office of Civil Rights and reinstating guidance for students with disabilities and English learners.
Assessments, in his view, should be treated as useful diagnostics rather than tools to punish educators.
Many families value choice for its own sake, so Democrats should offer better choices within the public sector.
Republicans should talk more about equity and Democrats more about excellence, which he sees as complementary.
quotes: Something missing is more than a passing nod to education and school improvement.

Defense should not mean preservation or restoration of the status quo. As I wrote last December in my piece about some of Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer’s final priorities in office: defending education means improving education.
Democrats should also insist that any private schools funded under the credit follow all federal testing and accountability provisions required of public schools.
It also means reckoning with the progressive temptation to treat educational measurement itself as inherently suspect.

The answer to an increasingly privatized delivery system of services for kids and families shouldn’t just be “don’t privatize it.” It should be building public institutions good enough that families actually want to choose them.
As I’ve written before, Republicans should be talking more about educational equity, and Democrats should be talking more about educational excellence.
